scenes.title: The question hidden in two boards
scenes.summary: Your 72 in and 63.5 in members are already telling us the sphere.
scenes.purpose: Your 72 in and 63.5 in members are already telling us the sphere.
narration: A 2V dome does not ask its two strut classes to be in the golden ratio.
It inherits phi in the parent icosahedron, then changes the edge geometry
when straight midpoints are projected back to a sphere.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Why domes triangulate
scenes.summary: A triangle carries load without changing shape; a square needs a brace.
scenes.purpose: A triangle carries load without changing shape; a square needs a brace.
narration: Push the top node: the force resolves into axial paths along the edges.
Triangulation trades bending-prone panels for a network of tension and
compression members. Real joints and foundations still require engineering.
equations: geometry explains form; engineering sizes members
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The five regular starting points
scenes.summary: The icosahedron wins because twenty small faces begin closest to a sphere.
scenes.purpose: The icosahedron wins because twenty small faces begin closest to a sphere.
narration: Each Platonic solid has one regular face type and one vertex arrangement.
More evenly distributed vertices mean a smaller correction when we project
the surface outward. The icosahedron gives twenty equilateral launch pads.
equations: 2V means: divide every parent edge into 2 segments
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Where the golden ratio really lives
scenes.summary: Phi builds the twelve parent vertices—not the finished strut ratio.
scenes.purpose: Phi builds the twelve parent vertices—not the finished strut ratio.
narration: The coordinate families (0, ±1, ±phi), (±1, ±phi, 0), and
(±phi, 0, ±1) place twelve points at one common radius.
Any neighboring pair is exactly 2 units apart before normalization.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Put the icosahedron on a unit sphere
scenes.summary: One division turns raw coordinates into reusable chord factors.
scenes.purpose: One division turns raw coordinates into reusable chord factors.
narration: Normalize each vertex by its distance from the origin.
Now the sphere radius is exactly one. Every measured edge is a multiplier
that can later be scaled to inches, feet, meters, or any other unit.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Split every parent edge in half
scenes.summary: Thirty parent edges create thirty new midpoint candidates.
scenes.purpose: Thirty parent edges create thirty new midpoint candidates.
narration: The arithmetic midpoint is easy: average the two endpoint vectors.
But that point lies inside the sphere. Leaving it there makes a faceted
icosahedron subdivision—not a geodesic sphere.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Project the midpoints outward
scenes.summary: Normalization is the exact radial projection back to the sphere.
scenes.purpose: Normalization is the exact radial projection back to the sphere.
narration: Each midpoint travels on a ray from the origin until its radius is one.
The new point changes the chord distances inside every subdivided face.
That single operation is where the two finished lengths appear.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Measure and group every chord
scenes.summary: 120 sphere edges collapse into exactly two numerical classes.
scenes.purpose: 120 sphere edges collapse into exactly two numerical classes.
narration: SHORT connects a parent vertex to a projected midpoint.
LONG connects two projected midpoints. Color grouping is numerical:
equal lengths receive equal colors—no letter convention is required.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Four routes to the same answer
scenes.summary: Coordinates, dot products, central angles, and the chord formula agree.
scenes.purpose: Coordinates, dot products, central angles, and the chord formula agree.
narration: Coordinate route: subtract endpoint vectors and take the magnitude.
Angle route: theta = acos(u dot v), then chord = 2R sin(theta/2).
Law of cosines, a spreadsheet, Python, and CAD must reproduce the same values.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Audit the 72 in / 63.5 in dome
scenes.summary: Your ratio is close; the two measurements imply radii only fractions apart.
scenes.purpose: Your ratio is close; the two measurements imply radii only fractions apart.
narration: Use each member independently to estimate radius, then use a least-squares
fit when both measurements contain cutting, hub, or tape error.
Center-to-center geometry must be separated from physical cut length.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: From radius to a cut list
scenes.summary: Scale the unit model once; then apply a documented connector deduction.
scenes.purpose: Scale the unit model once; then apply a documented connector deduction.
narration: A hemisphere contains 65 unique structural edges and 40 triangular faces.
The theoretical lengths are hub-center to hub-center. Tube, timber, tabs,
and commercial hubs each need their own verified end allowance.
equations: center length = chord factor x R
cut length = center length - connector deduction
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Panels, hubs, and build sequence
scenes.summary: Two triangle families repeat; hub angles are connector-system dependent.
scenes.purpose: Two triangle families repeat; hub angles are connector-system dependent.
narration: Make full-size gauges for SHORT and LONG, batch-cut, and label every part.
Dry-build repeating triangles before raising rings from the base upward.
PVC, timber, and tube share centerlines—not end cuts or structural capacity.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Close the measurement loop
scenes.summary: A good build is calculated, fabricated, measured, and corrected.
scenes.purpose: A good build is calculated, fabricated, measured, and corrected.
narration: Check member gauges, base decagon diagonals, hub-center radius, and level.
Small repeated errors accumulate around a ring. Correct them before the apex.
For occupied or load-bearing structures, use local code and an engineer.
equations: check: length -> triangle -> ring -> radius -> height
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The whole transformation
scenes.summary: Phi chooses the parent points; projection chooses the finished members.
scenes.purpose: Phi chooses the parent points; projection chooses the finished members.
narration: Raw phi coordinates become a normalized icosahedron.
Midpoints move outward, two chord factors emerge, and one scale factor
turns the unit geometry into a buildable 2V dome.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: What we are actually building
scenes.summary: One dome, twenty feet across, from two boards you already own.
scenes.purpose: One dome, twenty feet across, from two boards you already own.
narration: Before any mathematics, here is the finished thing, drawn to scale with a
six foot person beside it. Twenty feet across, ten feet to the crown, about
three hundred square feet of floor. Everything in the next half hour is in
service of that object: where its two strut lengths come from, how to cut
them, how to join them, how to stand them up, and how to know you got it
right.
equations: one radius scales the whole building
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The five words we will keep using
scenes.summary: Hub, strut, panel, chord factor, frequency. Learn them on the real thing.
scenes.purpose: Hub, strut, panel, chord factor, frequency. Learn them on the real thing.
narration: A hub is a joint. A strut is a straight member between two hubs. A panel is
the triangle they enclose. A chord factor is a strut's length divided by the
radius, which is what lets one drawing serve every size of dome. And
frequency is how many times each edge of the parent shape was divided:
two, in this case, which is where two V comes from.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Why the whole thing is triangles
scenes.summary: A triangle cannot change shape without changing a side length.
scenes.purpose: A triangle cannot change shape without changing a side length.
narration: Push the top corner of a square frame and it folds over into a diamond; no
side got longer, the shape just moved. Do the same to a triangle and nothing
happens, because moving any corner would have to stretch a side. That is the
entire structural argument for a geodesic dome, and it is why the frame
carries load along its members rather than bending them.
equations: geometry explains the form; an engineer sizes the members
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Where the shape starts: the icosahedron
scenes.summary: Twenty equal triangles are the closest a regular solid gets to a sphere.
scenes.purpose: Twenty equal triangles are the closest a regular solid gets to a sphere.
narration: Of the five regular solids, the icosahedron has the most faces and the most
evenly spread corners, so it needs the least correction when you push it out
to a sphere. That is the only reason it is chosen. It gives twenty
equilateral launch pads and twelve corners, and every geodesic dome in
common use starts here.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Phi builds the twelve corners
scenes.summary: The golden ratio places the parent vertices. It is not the strut ratio.
scenes.purpose: The golden ratio places the parent vertices. It is not the strut ratio.
narration: The twelve corners of an icosahedron are three golden rectangles standing
at right angles to each other. That is where the golden ratio genuinely
lives in this shape. It is worth being precise about, because the ratio of
the two finished strut lengths is not phi, and expecting it to be has sent
a lot of people down the wrong path.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Put it on a sphere of radius one
scenes.summary: One division turns coordinates into numbers you can scale to any size.
scenes.purpose: One division turns coordinates into numbers you can scale to any size.
narration: Divide every corner by its distance from the centre and the solid now sits
on a sphere of radius exactly one. From here on, every length we measure is
a multiple of the radius, so the same drawing serves a garden dome and a
hangar. This is the single most useful move in the whole derivation.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Halve every edge
scenes.summary: Thirty parent edges give thirty midpoints, and they are all too close in.
scenes.purpose: Thirty parent edges give thirty midpoints, and they are all too close in.
narration: Take the midpoint of every one of the thirty edges. That is just the average
of the two ends, and it is easy. But those midpoints sit inside the sphere,
not on it, because a straight line between two points on a curved surface
always cuts the corner. Leave them there and you have a faceted lump, not a
dome.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Push the midpoints out to the sphere
scenes.summary: This one move is what creates the second strut length.
scenes.purpose: This one move is what creates the second strut length.
narration: Slide each midpoint straight out from the centre until it reaches the
sphere. Nothing else changes. But by moving those thirty points outward,
every triangle around them changes shape, and the edges that used to be
equal split into two different lengths. That is the whole origin of the two
cut lengths in your shopping list.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Two lengths, and nothing else
scenes.summary: One hundred and twenty edges collapse into exactly two numbers.
scenes.purpose: One hundred and twenty edges collapse into exactly two numbers.
narration: Measure every edge on the finished sphere and they fall into two groups and
only two. The shorter one runs from an original corner to a projected
midpoint. The longer one runs between two projected midpoints, and it comes
out to exactly one over phi, which is the one place the golden ratio does
show up in the answer.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Choosing your radius
scenes.summary: Floor grows with the square of the radius. Volume grows with the cube.
scenes.purpose: Floor grows with the square of the radius. Volume grows with the cube.
narration: Now pick a size, and pick it for a reason. Doubling the radius gives four
times the floor, eight times the volume, and four times the skin you have to
buy and waterproof. Headroom at the wall is the thing people underestimate:
at the very edge of a hemisphere there is none at all, which is what the
riser wall later in this lesson is for.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The dome is four rings and a crown
scenes.summary: Twenty-six hubs, in courses, at heights you can measure before you build.
scenes.purpose: Twenty-six hubs, in courses, at heights you can measure before you build.
narration: Cut the sphere in half and the hubs sort themselves into level courses: ten
on the ground, then two rings of five, then five more, then the single hub at
the top. Twenty-six joints in total. Those ring heights and diameters are
your check numbers during the raise, so write them on the drawing before you
start.
equations: every ring is a level circle you can measure
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Auditing the boards you already have
scenes.summary: Two measured members imply two radii. Fit them, do not average them.
scenes.purpose: Two measured members imply two radii. Fit them, do not average them.
narration: You measured seventy-two inches and sixty-three and a half. Each of those
implies a radius on its own, and they disagree slightly, because real
members contain cutting and measuring error. The right move is a least
squares fit that weights both, not picking whichever one you trust more.
That fit is the radius the rest of this lesson uses.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Choose the hub system before anything else
scenes.summary: The connector decides the deduction, and the deduction decides every cut.
scenes.purpose: The connector decides the deduction, and the deduction decides every cut.
narration: A steel star plate, a bevelled timber joint, and a drilled hub ball all
build the same geometry but they eat different amounts of strut. Choose the
system now, build one joint for real, and measure how much shorter the
members have to be. Everything downstream depends on that one measurement,
and no catalogue number is a substitute for it.
equations: hub system -> connector deduction -> every cut length
build one real joint and measure it
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Centre length is not cut length
scenes.summary: The geometry gives hub centres. The saw needs something shorter.
scenes.purpose: The geometry gives hub centres. The saw needs something shorter.
narration: Every number in the derivation is hub centre to hub centre, because that is
what the sphere is made of. The stick you cut has to be shorter by whatever
the two connectors occupy. Note that the deduction is the total across both
ends, not per end; halving it by mistake is one of the most common ways a
dome ends up refusing to close.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The end-cut angle is half the central angle
scenes.summary: One line of arithmetic gives you the angle the strut leaves the surface at.
scenes.purpose: One line of arithmetic gives you the angle the strut leaves the surface at.
narration: A strut is a chord across the sphere, so it dips below the surface between
its ends. The angle it makes with the surface at each end is exactly half
the central angle that chord subtends, and the central angle comes straight
out of the chord factor. That is the angle to tip a hub plate to, or to cut
a timber end back to, and there is one value per strut class.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The panel bevels
scenes.summary: Two panels fold along every interior strut, and there are only two fold angles.
scenes.purpose: Two panels fold along every interior strut, and there are only two fold angles.
narration: Where two panels meet along a strut they are not in the same plane; they
fold. If you are skinning with rigid sheets, the edge of each panel wants to
be planed to half that fold so the two faces meet cleanly. There are exactly
two fold angles in the whole dome, one along each strut class, which means
two saw settings and no thinking at the bench.
equations: two fold angles in the entire dome
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: How many kinds of joint
scenes.summary: Five hub types, and they are not interchangeable.
scenes.purpose: Five hub types, and they are not interchangeable.
narration: Grouping the hubs by how many struts arrive and at what angles gives a small
number of distinct types. Make a set for each type, keep them in separate
labelled boxes, and check one against a drawing before you make the rest.
The base hubs are the ones to make first, because they also have to take the
anchor bolts.
equations: hub type = strut count + splay angles
make one, check it, then make the batch
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Buying the stock
scenes.summary: Choose the stock length before the radius and the offcut nearly vanishes.
scenes.purpose: Choose the stock length before the radius and the offcut nearly vanishes.
narration: Here is a real cost that geometry lessons never mention. At this radius, a
standard eight foot stick yields exactly one strut and throws the rest away.
A sixteen foot stick yields several. The right time to notice that is while
the radius is still adjustable, because a small change in radius can move
you from one piece per stick to two.
equations: pieces per stick = floor((stock + kerf) / (cut + kerf))
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Cutting: a stop block and a master
scenes.summary: Cut every piece of one class before you move anything.
scenes.purpose: Cut every piece of one class before you move anything.
narration: Set a stop block for the first class and cut all of them without touching
the setting. Keep the very first good piece as a master gauge and compare
the rest to it rather than re-measuring with a tape, because a tape
introduces a new error every time you use it. Label each piece as it comes
off the saw. Then, and only then, move the stop.
equations: compare to a master, not to a tape
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The finished cut list
scenes.summary: Sixty-five members, two lengths, and a count you can hand to a shop.
scenes.purpose: Sixty-five members, two lengths, and a count you can hand to a shop.
narration: This is the whole order: thirty of the shorter class and thirty-five of the
longer, at the cut lengths we derived, plus the hub schedule. Add spares.
Two or three of each class costs very little and saves an entire afternoon
the first time a piece splits or a cut goes wrong.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Build the triangles flat, first
scenes.summary: Two triangle families repeat all forty times. Jig them on the ground.
scenes.purpose: Two triangle families repeat all forty times. Jig them on the ground.
narration: The dome contains only two kinds of triangle: thirty with two short sides
and one long, and ten with three long sides. Lay one of each out on a flat
floor, screw down blocks to make a jig, and assemble the rest inside the
jig. Every panel then comes out identical, and the raise turns into
bolting known-good pieces together rather than fitting each one.
equations: jig them flat before anything goes up
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Setting out the base
scenes.summary: A ten-sided ring, set out from the centre, checked on the diagonals.
scenes.purpose: A ten-sided ring, set out from the centre, checked on the diagonals.
narration: Drive a pin at the centre and swing the base radius to mark all ten hub
positions. Do not step around the ring measuring side to side, because every
small error then adds to the next one. When the ten are pegged, measure the
long diagonals: on a regular ten-sided ring they are all identical, so any
difference is telling you exactly where the setting out drifted.
equations: set out from the centre, every time
all five long diagonals are equal on a true ring
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Meeting the ground
scenes.summary: Piers, a ring beam, or a slab. Whichever you choose has to be level.
scenes.purpose: Piers, a ring beam, or a slab. Whichever you choose has to be level.
narration: A dome puts a concentrated outward-and-down load at each base hub, so the
foundation either has to catch each one individually with a pier, or tie
them all together with a ring beam or slab that resists the spread. The
structural choice is yours and your engineer's. The one non-negotiable is
that the ten bearing points end up on one level plane.
equations: base hubs push down and outward
pier, ring beam, or slab -- but level
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The riser wall
scenes.summary: The cheapest usable space a dome will ever sell you.
scenes.purpose: The cheapest usable space a dome will ever sell you.
narration: A hemisphere has no headroom at its edge, which makes the outer ring of
floor nearly useless. Stand the whole dome on a short vertical wall and every
point of the shell rises by that amount, so the perimeter becomes furniture
height or door height. It costs one ring of studs and it changes the plan
completely. Decide on it before you set out, because it changes the
foundation.
equations: the floor area does not change; the usable area does
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Raising it, one complete ring at a time
scenes.summary: Never build up one side. The shell is not stable until a ring closes.
scenes.purpose: Never build up one side. The shell is not stable until a ring closes.
narration: Bolt the base hubs down, then work upward in complete courses. A half-built
ring is a row of unstable triangles and it will lean; a closed ring is a
rigid hoop that holds its own shape. Prop each course until the one above it
closes. Measure the diameter across each finished ring in three directions
before you begin the next, and correct there rather than higher up.
equations: prop until the ring above closes
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Closing the crown
scenes.summary: If the last hub will not fit, the error is in the ring below it.
scenes.purpose: If the last hub will not fit, the error is in the ring below it.
narration: The top hub is where every accumulated millimetre finally arrives, so it is
the honest test of everything below. If the five struts will not reach it
cleanly, resist the urge to force them. Go back down and measure the ring
beneath: nearly always it is slightly out of round or slightly out of level,
and correcting it there is far quicker than fighting the crown.
equations: the crown reports the error, it does not cause it
5 SHORT struts meet at the apex
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: What an eighth of an inch actually does
scenes.summary: A ten-sided ring amplifies a strut error by exactly the golden ratio.
scenes.purpose: A ten-sided ring amplifies a strut error by exactly the golden ratio.
narration: Here is a number worth carrying around. If every base strut is one eighth of
an inch long, the base radius is out by phi times that, and the diameter by
twice again. The same golden ratio that placed the parent corners now
governs how your mistakes grow. It is not a large factor, but it is a
multiplier, and it explains why domes drift bigger rather than smaller.
equations: so radius error = phi x strut error
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The measurement loop
scenes.summary: Member, triangle, ring, radius, height. In that order, every time.
scenes.purpose: Member, triangle, ring, radius, height. In that order, every time.
narration: Check a member against the master gauge. Check a triangle on all three
corners. Check a ring on its diameter, three ways. Check the radius from the
centre pin to each hub. Check the apex height against the radius, because on
a true hemisphere they are the same number. Each check catches what the
previous one could hide, and doing them in order is what stops a small
error becoming a structural one.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Skinning it, rim upward
scenes.summary: Forty panels, laid so every lap sheds downhill, sealed at every hub.
scenes.purpose: Forty panels, laid so every lap sheds downhill, sealed at every hub.
narration: Start at the base and work up so each panel laps over the one below it,
exactly like roof shingles. Every hub is a junction of several panel corners
and those are the leak points, so flash or tape each one before the next
course covers it. Give the base a real drip edge that throws water clear of
the wall. A dome almost never fails structurally; it fails at its seams.
equations: a drip edge at the base is not optional
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Doors, windows, and what not to cut
scenes.summary: Take whole panels. Cutting a strut means replacing a load path.
scenes.purpose: Take whole panels. Cutting a strut means replacing a load path.
narration: The clean way to make an opening is to leave a panel out and frame the
triangle. The frame is untouched and the shell keeps working. If you must
make a bigger opening, head it with a member at least as strong as the ones
you removed and get that detail checked, because a dome carries load through
its net and a missing strut is a missing path, not just a missing stick.
equations: a cut strut needs its load path replaced
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The four things that actually go wrong
scenes.summary: None of them are geometry. All of them are avoidable.
scenes.purpose: None of them are geometry. All of them are avoidable.
narration: Domes rarely fail because the arithmetic was wrong. They fail because the
connector deduction was guessed instead of measured, because the base was
not level, because someone built up one side instead of in rings, or because
two similar-looking members got mixed up. Each of those is a habit, not a
calculation, and each is cheap to fix before you start and expensive after.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The dome with no hubs in it
scenes.summary: Forty complete triangles, and not one connector between them.
scenes.purpose: Forty complete triangles, and not one connector between them.
narration: Everything so far assumed a hub: a plate or a bracket that several struts
arrive at. There is another way to build the same sphere that has no hubs at
all. You make each of the forty triangles as a finished, closed triangle, and
then you bolt the triangles to each other edge to edge. Nothing meets at a
point any more. Every joint is now a lap between two flat sides.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Why it takes 120 struts, not 65
scenes.summary: Every shared edge now carries two struts instead of one.
scenes.purpose: Every shared edge now carries two struts instead of one.
narration: A hubbed dome has sixty-five struts because each edge is one member serving
the panels on both sides of it. A hubless dome gives each triangle its own
three members, so an edge between two triangles ends up with two struts lying
face to face, bolted through. Fifty-five edges are shared like that. Ten more
sit on the rim with nothing on the other side. Two times fifty-five, plus ten,
is one hundred and twenty, and that is the whole frame.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The compound cut
scenes.summary: Two angles at once, on the same pass, on every single end.
scenes.purpose: Two angles at once, on the same pass, on every single end.
narration: Here is the part that stops people. Each strut end needs the saw swung to a
mitre, so the strut meets its neighbour in the plane of its own triangle, and
the blade tilted to a bevel, so the face lies flat against the triangle next
door. Those two settings are not applied one after the other. They happen on
the same cut, which is what compound means, and getting one right while the
other is wrong gives you a part that looks correct and fits nothing.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Every angle you need is past the stop
scenes.summary: The geometry is easy. The tool is the problem.
scenes.purpose: The geometry is easy. The tool is the problem.
narration: Now the sting. The mitres this dome asks for run from about fifty-six degrees
to about sixty-two degrees away from square, and a common mitre saw stops at
fifty. Not one of the settings this dome needs is on the scale. The way
through is that a mitre and its complement are the same cut approached from
the other face: swing the saw to the complement instead, which lands between
twenty-seven and thirty-four degrees, and rotate the workpiece a quarter turn
in a sled. Same joint, reachable setting. Build the sled first, before you cut
anything you care about.
equations: complement: 27.8 to 34.4 deg, and turn the part
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The tube around the bottom
scenes.summary: This one started with a badly ventilated workshop.
scenes.purpose: This one started with a badly ventilated workshop.
narration: A dome has an unhelpful habit: warm air and anything it carries rises to the
apex and stays there. Weld inside one and you are standing in a chimney with
no flue. The fix that came out of that is a tube running right around the
base, with a blower on it, so the whole perimeter becomes one duct instead of
the building having a single extract point somewhere on one wall.
equations: ring main = one duct all the way round
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Run it either way
scenes.summary: The same tube and the same fan make two different buildings.
scenes.purpose: The same tube and the same fan make two different buildings.
narration: Push air in at the ring and it leaves through the shell, carrying fumes out
through the whole surface at once instead of dragging them past your face to
one vent. Reverse it and you draw outside air inward through the shell, which
warms it against the structure on the way in and recovers heat you would
otherwise throw away. That second mode has a real name in building science:
dynamic insulation, or a breathing wall. Same hardware. One switch.
equations: push: purge fumes through the whole surface
pull: incoming air warmed by the shell
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The wall as the filter
scenes.summary: The shell is so large that the air barely crawls through it.
scenes.purpose: The shell is so large that the air barely crawls through it.
narration: Here is why the idea is interesting rather than merely odd. A ten foot dome
holds about two hundred and sixty cubic feet of air behind about fifteen
square metres of wall. Even purging hard, at forty air changes an hour, the
air crosses that wall at about one foot per minute. A draught you can feel
starts somewhere near forty. So the entire envelope becomes a filter face and
nobody inside feels a thing, because the flow is spread over the whole
building instead of rushing past one grille.
equations: through the wall at about 1 ft/min
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: What would actually decide it
scenes.summary: The flow numbers are computed. The wall is not proven.
scenes.purpose: The flow numbers are computed. The wall is not proven.
narration: Being straight about this: the geometry and the airflow above are calculated,
and the idea that a strut lattice makes a good distributed plenum at building
scale is untested. Five things decide it. Direction, because pushing warm wet
air outward through a cold wall condenses it inside that wall and rots the
shell where you cannot see it. A sealed fibreglass skin cannot breathe at all,
so the permeable band has to be designed in rather than hoped for. And a
filter you cannot reach is a filter you will never change.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Forty panels from one sheet
scenes.summary: The whole shell, nested onto a single ten by five foot sheet.
scenes.purpose: The whole shell, nested onto a single ten by five foot sheet.
narration: Different build entirely. Forget struts: cut the forty triangles as solid
panels and join them edge to edge. The question is how big a dome you can get
off one sheet. Congruent triangles pair into parallelograms, and
parallelograms strip-pack with no waste along a row, because the slope of one
is filled by the next. Solving that packing against a ten by five sheet, with
a real kerf and a real edge margin, gives a radius of about thirty-one inches.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The sub-two-thousand-dollar storm shelter
scenes.summary: Sixty-two inches across, thirty-one inches tall. It is not cozy.
scenes.purpose: Sixty-two inches across, thirty-one inches tall. It is not cozy.
narration: That sheet buys a shell about five feet across with thirty-one inches of
headroom and twenty-one square feet of floor. You do not stand up in it. You
do not really sit up in it either. I have been inside it, so nobody needs to
tell me it is not cozy. It is a hole you can afford, above ground, that a
laser can cut in an afternoon. And if you want it habitable rather than
survivable, the riser wall from earlier fixes it for almost nothing: five
inches of riser gets you sitting upright, and forty-one inches gets you
standing, without recutting a single panel. If you have seen a shelter cheaper
than this that a person can actually get into, message the channel. I would
genuinely like to study it.
equations: 62 in across, 31 in headroom, 21 sq ft
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The franken-dome
scenes.summary: One hundred and twenty struts, and no two of them alike.
scenes.purpose: One hundred and twenty struts, and no two of them alike.
narration: Last one, and it is an experiment rather than a recommendation. I wanted to
know how fast a dome goes up if you stop caring what the struts are. Round
logs, quarter-cut pieces, wedges, square stock, rectangular offcuts, whatever
the chainsaw produced that day. Every section has a different effective
centreline, so not one joint lands where the geometry says it should.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Why the lumpy one stays up
scenes.summary: The errors have nowhere to accumulate, and the skin covers the rest.
scenes.purpose: The errors have nowhere to accumulate, and the skin covers the rest.
narration: It should not work and it does, for two reasons. A closed triangulated shell
is enormously redundant: every triangle is rigid by itself, so an error at one
joint is absorbed by the two hundred around it instead of walking around a
ring the way it does in a precise dome. What you get is a lumpy brain of a
frame that is near the sphere without being on it. Then the sheathing does the
rest. A monolithic skin bonded over the outside spans the slack and gives back
the shell action the sloppiness cost you.
equations: every triangle rigid on its own
the skin returns the shell action
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Borrowing strength from the site
scenes.summary: Four trees did the work the tolerance did not.
scenes.purpose: Four trees did the work the tolerance did not.
narration: It went up between four trees, and that was not an accident. Cable overhead,
tied back into the trunks, meant the frame never had to be self-supporting
while it was going together, and the trees kept taking a share afterwards.
Covered in clear plastic, it stood through half a year of weather with no
complaints before I took it down on purpose. That is eighteen times its own
build time, which is the only durability number I actually have.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: What it cost, and the crown I award myself
scenes.summary: A chainsaw, a tarp, and rather a lot of screws.
scenes.purpose: A chainsaw, a tarp, and rather a lot of screws.
narration: The ledger. One hundred and twenty brackets, eight screws in each, which is
nine hundred and sixty screws. Two bolts through every edge, so a hundred and
thirty bolts and two hundred and sixty washers. Ten days, four triangles a
day. The timber was free and the tarp was nearly free; the hardware was the
real cost, and that is the part worth spending on, because heavy bolts get
unbolted and reused on the next and better dome. That is investment that never
goes obsolete. As far as I can tell nobody has put this particular method on
the internet before, which by my own reckoning and absolutely nobody else's
crowns me sovereign of a hobo commune that does not exist, somewhere pleasant
with relaxed local statutes. The crown is imaginary. The building was not.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The whole thing, once more, quickly
scenes.summary: From the golden ratio to a building you can stand inside.
scenes.purpose: From the golden ratio to a building you can stand inside.
narration: Phi places twelve corners. Normalising puts them on a unit sphere. Halving
every edge and pushing the midpoints out gives two chord factors. One radius
turns those into two cut lengths. A connector deduction turns those into saw
settings. Jigs turn saw settings into identical triangles, rings turn
triangles into a shell, and a skin turns a shell into a room. Every number
came from the geometry, and every one of them can be recomputed instead of
trusted.
equations: phi -> icosahedron -> 2V -> SHORT + LONG -> R -> cut list -> building
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Two angles, one stick
scenes.summary: Every strut carries two completely different angles, on two machines.
scenes.purpose: Every strut carries two completely different angles, on two machines.
narration: This is the hardest operation in the whole dome, and it is worth being
precise about why. Every strut carries two angles that have nothing to do
with each other. There is a bevel that runs the entire length of the stick,
and there is a mitre at each end. The bevel decides how this triangle meets
the triangle next door. The mitre decides how this strut meets the other two
struts of its own triangle. Get one right and the other wrong and you have a
part that looks perfect on the bench and fits absolutely nothing.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Why it takes two saws
scenes.summary: Each machine can only do the cut the other one cannot.
scenes.purpose: Each machine can only do the cut the other one cannot.
narration: A table saw rips along the length of a board and cannot sensibly crosscut a
long stick at sixty degrees. A mitre saw crosscuts ends and cannot rip at
all. That is the entire reason this job needs two machines. It is not
fussiness and it is not showing off. There is no single setup on either saw
that produces a finished strut.
equations: table saw: rips, cannot crosscut at 62 deg
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: One width, one session
scenes.summary: Every angle after this is measured from the edge of the board.
scenes.purpose: Every angle after this is measured from the edge of the board.
narration: Before any angle at all: rip every stick to one width, in one session, with
the fence untouched. Every angle downstream is measured from the edge of the
board, so if the boards are not identical in width, nothing after this point
can be right, and no amount of care at the mitre saw will rescue it. This is
the least interesting step and the one that quietly decides the outcome.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Mark the mating edge
scenes.summary: Only one long edge gets the bevel. Mark it before anything moves.
scenes.purpose: Only one long edge gets the bevel. Mark it before anything moves.
narration: Only one long edge of each strut gets bevelled: the one that will lie
against the neighbouring triangle. Mark that edge on every stick in the pile
before a single one goes near the blade. Bevelling the wrong edge is the
most common way to manufacture a large quantity of mirror-image firewood,
and it is completely invisible until you try to assemble.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Setting the blade tilt
scenes.summary: Do not trust the saw's own scale.
scenes.purpose: Do not trust the saw's own scale.
narration: Now the table saw. Tilt the blade to the bevel for this strut class. Do not
trust the scale cast into the saw; it is a starting point, not a
measurement. And set the blade height after the tilt, never before, because
a tilted blade has to travel further to cross the same thickness and a height
set square will not come through.
equations: set the tilt first, the height second
a tilted blade needs more height
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Proving the tilt
scenes.summary: Rip two offcuts, put them together, and read twice the error.
scenes.purpose: Rip two offcuts, put them together, and read twice the error.
narration: Here is how you know the tilt is right before you commit the pile. Rip two
offcuts at the setting, then put the two cut faces together and measure the
pair. If the tilt is correct the pair closes to exactly the fold the dome
wants along that strut. And because the pair carries both errors, anything
too small to see in a single piece is obvious in the double.
equations: the pair reads the dome's own dihedral
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The rip
scenes.summary: One pass, full length, marked edge against the fence.
scenes.purpose: One pass, full length, marked edge against the fence.
narration: Featherboard before the blade, push stick past it, marked edge against the
fence for every stick without exception. One pass, the full length. This is
the easy half of the job: the bevel the dome needs is nowhere near the
forty-five degrees the saw can tilt to, so the machine is never the limit
here. Consistency is.
equations: the tilt is well inside the saw's range
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The saw runs out of scale
scenes.summary: Swing it to its stop and it is still not enough.
scenes.purpose: Swing it to its stop and it is still not enough.
narration: Now the ends, and now the problem. Swing the mitre saw as far as it goes.
A common saw stops at about fifty degrees from square. The mitres this dome
wants start at fifty-five and a half and run past sixty-two. Not one of the
settings this dome needs is on the scale. The saw is not badly made. The
angle is simply outside what a mitre saw is built to do.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: One angle, two names
scenes.summary: Measure it from the blade instead of from square.
scenes.purpose: Measure it from the blade instead of from square.
narration: The way out is not a trick, it is a change of reference. An angle measured
from square and its complement measured from the blade describe the same
cut. Sixty-two degrees from square is twenty-seven point eight degrees from
the blade. So stop trying to make the saw's table reach the number, and
build a fence that holds the work at the complement instead.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The sled
scenes.summary: A crosscut sled with its fence built to the complement.
scenes.purpose: A crosscut sled with its fence built to the complement.
narration: So the ends get cut on a crosscut sled on the table saw. Two runners in the
mitre slots with no slop at all, a flat base, and a fence set to the
complement angle referenced off the blade. Build the sled first. Prove it.
Only then cut a part you care about. Every strut in the dome passes over
this one fence, so every error built into it is an error repeated two
hundred and forty times.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Proving the fence
scenes.summary: The five-cut method makes an invisible error measurable.
scenes.purpose: The five-cut method makes an invisible error measurable.
narration: You cannot check a fence this critical with a combination square. Use the
five-cut method: cut a scrap four times, rotating it a quarter turn between
cuts, then slice a fifth strip off and measure that strip at both ends. The
four cuts multiply the fence error by four, so a difference of five
thousandths across a twenty inch strip means the fence is out by less than
four thousandths of a degree. That is a level of proof you simply cannot get
by eye.
equations: four cuts multiply the error by four
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The relief lap and the stop block
scenes.summary: The blade has to finish the cut flush, so the fence gets cut away.
scenes.purpose: The blade has to finish the cut flush, so the fence gets cut away.
narration: Two details on the sled that decide whether it works. First, the strut sits
against the fence with one end projecting past it, and the blade has to
finish that cut flush, so the fence is cut away at the blade path. Cut that
lap once, with the sled in the exact position it will always be used in.
Second, length comes from a stop block clamped to the sled, never from a
pencil line. Two hundred and forty ends measured individually will drift.
Two hundred and forty ends against one block will not.
equations: relief lap: cut once, in position
stop block, never a tape measure
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The first end
scenes.summary: Bevelled edge down, butted to the stop, one pass all the way through.
scenes.purpose: Bevelled edge down, butted to the stop, one pass all the way through.
narration: Bevelled edge down and against the fence. Marked face up. Strut butted hard
to the stop block, the end projecting over the lap. One pass, all the way
through, and let the blade come to a stop before you lift the work. That is
the compound cut: the sled is holding the mitre and the stick is already
carrying its bevel, so both angles arrive on the same pass.
equations: butted to the stop, one pass
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Turn it, do not flip it
scenes.summary: The second end is not a mirror of the first.
scenes.purpose: The second end is not a mirror of the first.
narration: Now the second end, and this is where a whole afternoon can go. The second
end is not a mirror of the first. Rotate the strut end for end about its own
long axis, the way the sled was built for, so the bevelled edge stays on the
same side of the dome. If you flip it face over face instead, you mirror the
part. It will look completely correct lying on the bench and it will refuse
to close a triangle, and you will not find out until assembly.
equations: turn end for end about the long axis
flipping face over face mirrors the part
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Batch by setting
scenes.summary: Six setting changes, not two hundred and forty.
scenes.purpose: Six setting changes, not two hundred and forty.
narration: Cut every end that shares a setting before you change anything. Changing a
setting is where error enters the job, so change it as few times as the work
allows. Six setups cover all two hundred and forty ends in the dome. Sorted
by setting that is six careful changes. Sorted by triangle it is a change
every couple of minutes for two days, and every one of them a chance to be
slightly wrong.
equations: batch by setting, never by triangle
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Dry-fit one triangle
scenes.summary: Three struts on a flat floor, no fasteners.
scenes.purpose: Three struts on a flat floor, no fasteners.
narration: Before you cut the rest of the pile, dry-assemble one triangle. Three struts
on a flat floor, no fasteners at all. If it closes with no gap at any corner
and lies flat, your settings are right and you can cut with confidence. If
it does not, you have lost three sticks instead of the whole pile, and you
still have the setting in front of you to correct.
equations: no gap at any corner, and it lies flat
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The five ways it goes wrong
scenes.summary: Every one of them looks correct until assembly.
scenes.purpose: Every one of them looks correct until assembly.
narration: Five failures, and they share a nasty property: every one produces a part
that looks right. Bevel on the wrong edge. Setting the sled to the mitre
instead of its complement. Flipping instead of turning. A stop block that
has walked under repeated impact. And a blade set to a height that was
correct before you tilted it. Check the block against a reference stick
every twenty cuts, and check the height after every tilt change.
equations: all five produce parts that look correct
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The whole sequence
scenes.summary: Two machines, one jig, six settings, two hundred and forty ends.
scenes.purpose: Two machines, one jig, six settings, two hundred and forty ends.
narration: Rip everything to one width. Mark the mating edge. Tilt, prove the tilt with
a pair of offcuts, and rip the bevel full length. Build the sled to the
complement and prove it with the five-cut method. Cut the relief lap and set
the stop block. Then cut, turn, cut, batching by setting, and dry-fit one
triangle before you trust the rest. Two machines, one jig, six settings, two
hundred and forty ends. Do it in that order and the hardest part of the dome
becomes the most repetitive part instead.
equations: rip -> mark -> tilt -> rip -> sled -> lap -> cut -> turn -> dry-fit
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Cold Hook
scenes.summary: How dare you enter the High Council Dome without my permission!
scenes.purpose: How dare you enter the High Council Dome without my permission!
narration: How dare you enter the High Council Dome without my permission!
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Escalation
scenes.summary: I built these structural struts! This entire dome falls apart without my key!
scenes.purpose: I built these structural struts! This entire dome falls apart without my key!
narration: I built these structural struts! This entire dome falls apart without my key!
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Reveal
scenes.summary: He speaks the truth, Aurelia. He is the rightful master of the Vance Network.
scenes.purpose: He speaks the truth, Aurelia. He is the rightful master of the Vance Network.
narration: He speaks the truth, Aurelia. He is the rightful master of the Vance Network.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Cliffhanger
scenes.summary: Too late, old man! The explosive charges are already armed across the outer facets!
scenes.purpose: Too late, old man! The explosive charges are already armed across the outer facets!
narration: Too late, old man! The explosive charges are already armed across the outer facets!
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The franken-dome
scenes.summary: One hundred and twenty struts, and no two of them alike.
scenes.purpose: One hundred and twenty struts, and no two of them alike.
narration: This is an experiment, not a recommendation, and it is documented here
because nobody seems to have written it down. The question was simple: how
fast does a dome go up if you stop caring what the struts are? Not cheaper
struts. Not rougher struts. Struts with no specification at all, beyond
being roughly the right length.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Whatever the chainsaw made
scenes.summary: Round, quarter-sawn, wedge, square, rectangular. All in the same dome.
scenes.purpose: Round, quarter-sawn, wedge, square, rectangular. All in the same dome.
narration: Round logs still in the bark. Quarter-sawn pieces off a milling jig. Wedges
that were offcuts of something else. Square stock, rectangular stock,
whatever came off the pile that day. They are not interchangeable in any
engineering sense: every one of those sections has its centreline in a
different place, so no two joints in the whole dome are the same joint.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Where a bracket comes from
scenes.summary: A flat band of washing machine casing, drilled.
scenes.purpose: A flat band of washing machine casing, drilled.
narration: The joints are the interesting part. Every one is a bracket I made, and
every bracket started as a flat band sheared out of a scrapped washing
machine. That casing is galvanised sheet in a gauge that is genuinely
structural at this size, it is free, it is already flat, and there is a
great deal of it in the world. Shear a band, drill six or eight holes in
it, and that is the whole component.
equations: shear a band, drill 6 to 8 holes
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: One fold makes it a joint
scenes.summary: Bend it in half and it becomes a V.
scenes.purpose: Bend it in half and it becomes a V.
narration: Then one fold, straight down the middle, and the band becomes a V. That is
the entire bracket. No welding, no castings, no bought connectors. And
because you are bending it yourself, the fold angle is simply whatever that
particular corner turned out to be, which on a frame like this is never the
angle on the drawing. The bracket adapts to the joint instead of the joint
having to match the bracket. That is the trick, and it is why the method
tolerates such rough stock.
equations: the bracket adapts to the joint, not the other way round
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Four screws into each strut
scenes.summary: Two struts, one V, eight screws.
scenes.purpose: Two struts, one V, eight screws.
narration: In place it works like this. The V straddles the corner, one leg down each
strut. Four screws through the leg into the first strut, four more into the
second, so eight screws per bracket. Four in shear along a leg is a
genuinely stiff connection, and it fails gradually and visibly rather than
suddenly, which for a structure you are experimenting with is exactly the
behaviour you want.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: One triangle at a time
scenes.summary: Three sticks, three brackets, twenty-four screws.
scenes.purpose: Three sticks, three brackets, twenty-four screws.
narration: The unit of work is one triangle: three sticks, three brackets, twenty-four
screws. You build them flat on the ground, which means no ladder work and no
holding anything overhead. Forty of those and the dome is a pile of finished
triangles waiting to be stood up.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Nothing lands where it should
scenes.summary: Green is the geometry. Red is where the stick actually put it.
scenes.purpose: Green is the geometry. Red is where the stick actually put it.
narration: Here is the honest picture of what you get. The green points are where the
geometry says every hub belongs. The red lines show where the sticks
actually put them. Not one joint in the dome lands on the sphere. Some are
out by a quarter of an inch, some by more, and every single one of those
errors is a different error because every stick is a different stick.
equations: not one joint on the sphere
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: And then it settles
scenes.summary: Pull it together and the whole frame shares the error out.
scenes.purpose: Pull it together and the whole frame shares the error out.
narration: Now watch what happens when you actually pull it together and stand it up.
The frame settles. Every triangle is individually rigid, so a joint that
wants to sit proud is held by the two around it, and the error gets shared
out across the whole shell instead of accumulating around a ring the way it
does in a precise dome. That redundancy is not a nice property here. It is
the only reason the thing stands at all.
equations: the error is shared, not accumulated
redundancy is what makes it possible
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The sheathing takes up the rest
scenes.summary: A monolithic skin spans slack the frame never lost.
scenes.purpose: A monolithic skin spans slack the frame never lost.
narration: What is left after settling is a lumpy brain of a frame that is near the
sphere without being on it. The sheathing finishes the job. A skin bonded
over the outside bridges every remaining gap and gives back the shell action
the sloppiness cost. Once it is on, the structure behaves far more like the
skin than like the frame, which is the whole reason the frame is allowed to
be this bad.
equations: the skin returns the shell action
the structure becomes the skin, not the frame
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Borrowing from the site
scenes.summary: Four trees did the work the tolerance did not.
scenes.purpose: Four trees did the work the tolerance did not.
narration: It went up between four trees, and that was not an accident. Cable overhead
tied back into the trunks meant the frame never had to be self-supporting
while it was going together, and the trees kept taking a share afterwards.
Covered in clear plastic, it stood through half a year of weather before I
took it down deliberately. That is eighteen times its own build time, which
is the only durability number I actually have.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The parts list
scenes.summary: One hundred and twenty brackets, nine hundred and sixty screws.
scenes.purpose: One hundred and twenty brackets, nine hundred and sixty screws.
narration: The whole ledger. One hundred and twenty brackets, folded by hand from
scrap. Nine hundred and sixty screws. One hundred and twenty struts of no
particular description. Ten days, which is four triangles and about a
hundred screws a day. The timber was free and the brackets were free. The
screws were the entire material cost of the structure.
equations: the screws were the whole material cost
