The bevel is identical on every member in the dome, and it is exactly half the sector angle. It is set by how the log was split, not by where the member sits in the shell, so you set it once and never touch it again.

And the mitre takes only three values across all hundred and twenty members, all of them inside the swing of a common saw. So the cradle holds one sawn face down with the point against a fence, the bevel stays locked, and there are three stops.

narration: A conventional frame would put one member on the edge between two panels and bolt both to it. This one does not.
Each panel carries its own member along that edge, so the shell has two. That sounds wasteful and is the opposite.

It means a panel is complete before it meets anything, and it means the joint between panels is a connection between two finished things rather than a shared dependency. It also doubles the wood on every interior edge, which is where the structural argument later gets its margin from.

One sitting produced twelve wedges in two hours and burned ten dollars of fuel and bar oil. A separate sitting cut forty-two feet of rip at six inches of depth in one hour, on two tanks of fuel and two of bar oil, including a chain sharpening.

Those two sessions counted different things, which is what makes them worth having. Divide one by the other and you get feet of cut per finished wedge, and the geometry can predict that number independently.

scenes.title: What one wedge is worth
scenes.summary: Priced against the sticks it would take to replace it.
scenes.purpose: Priced against the sticks it would take to replace it.
narration: A wedge is not one two-by-four. It is thicker, so comparing them piece for piece would quietly build a weaker dome and call it cheaper.

The honest comparison is by cross-section: how many dressed studs you would have to lay alongside one wedge to match the wood in it. At the trunk diameter I actually cut, that number is close to three, and the estimate I have been using for planning is two.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: The rule of thumb, checked
scenes.summary: Two ways to price a wedge, and how far apart they land.
scenes.purpose: Two ways to price a wedge, and how far apart they land.
narration: The rule of thumb multiplies a conservative section factor by the price of an eight-foot stud section. The strict version uses the computed section and also corrects for the fact that a six-foot wedge is shorter than an eight-foot stud.
They should not agree as closely as they do. The conservative multiplier and the generous length happen to cancel almost exactly, which is a piece of luck rather than a method.
Either way, an afternoon of ripping produces a specific number of dollars of wood I would otherwise have had to buy.
equations: a 2x4x16 untreated pine is $8.88 on the rack, $10.00 with tax
one 1/8 wedge of a 12 in trunk has 14.14 in2 of section
the estimate on site was 2.5 x
the multiplier actually used for planning was 2.0 x -- lower than both
STRICT, counting section AND the length difference:
at 5 wedges an hour that is $50.00/hour gross, $45.00 after fuel
one 6-hour afternoon: 30 wedges, $300 of wood, $30 of fuel
A conservative multiplier and a generous length cancel almost exactly, so both methods say the same thing: about $45 an hour, in wood you would otherwise have had to buy.

scenes.title: The part nobody counts
scenes.summary: Culls, trips, hours and the boards that never make it.
scenes.purpose: Culls, trips, hours and the boards that never make it.
narration: A shelf price is not what lumber costs you. There is the drive there and back, the time picking through a rack for boards that are not bowed, the queue, the loading and the unloading.
There are the boards you buy and then reject anyway, and the ones that split or soak between the yard and the site. You paid for those too.
My chainsaw's fuel bill sits roughly where the truck's fuel bill would have been, so it is not the consumables that differ. It is everything attached to them.

scenes.title: The same frame, bought
scenes.summary: Enough studs to match the section, plus everything attached.
scenes.purpose: Enough studs to match the section, plus everything attached.
narration: This prices the store-bought route properly: enough dressed studs to match the cross-section the wedges provide, not one stud per member, because those are not the same building. Then the culls, the transit losses, the truck runs and the hours those runs take.
Every one of those is an estimate and every one is on the side of the comparison I am arguing against. The cutting column is the measured rate and the measured fuel, and it contains no trips at all.
equations: to match the section 120 wedges provide you would need 2.69 dressed studs alongside each one
/ 16 ft = 121 sticks of actual wood needed
10 % bought and rejected -- bowed, twisted, wet, split
3 % lost to handling and weather on the way
so you buy 139 sticks, 18 of which become firewood ($176)
4 truck loads x 40 mi = 160 mi at $0.55/mi = $88
and 6.0 h of driving, picking, queuing, loading and unloading = $150 of time
CUT: 24 h of ripping, $120 of fuel and oil, no trips at all
The chainsaw's fuel bill roughly replaces the truck's, so the real difference is $1356 of cash that never leaves, and a stack of wood that was already on the property.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: The number that depends on the tree
scenes.summary: The one figure that could sink all of this.
scenes.purpose: The one figure that could sink all of this.
narration: A raw sector is literally one eighth of the tree. Whether that is a stronger stick than a two-by-four is not a yes or a no; it is a question about diameter.

Cross-section grows with the square of the radius and bending stiffness grows with the cube, so there is a trunk diameter where the sector overtakes the stud, and below it the sector loses. I am going to give you that crossover diameter rather than a slogan, because it is the one number that could sink this whole method and it deserves to be said out loud.
equations: the trees being cut are 12-15 in

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: Section properties, and the crossover
scenes.summary: Area, second moment and section modulus, at both diameters.
scenes.purpose: Area, second moment and section modulus, at both diameters.
narration: These are not looked up. The sector outline comes out of the same code that builds the dome, and the area and second moments are integrated around that polygon, checked against the closed form for a circular sector.
At the eight-inch trunk the simulator defaults to, one wedge is the weaker stick in bending. At the twelve-inch trunks I actually cut, it is comfortably the stronger one.
The crossover is solved for rather than asserted. None of this is an engineer's design check.
A real build needs species, grade, moisture and somebody who will sign it. This is the geometry underneath that conversation.
equations: a raw sector is literally 1/8 of the tree, and how strong that is depends entirely on how big the tree was.
= 120 % of a dressed 2x4's area but only 67 % of its bending
AT THE 12 IN TRUNKS ACTUALLY BEING CUT:
= 269 % of a dressed 2x4's area and 226 % of its bending
section grows with the square of the radius and bending with the
cube, so there is a diameter where the sector overtakes the stud:
more area than a dressed 2x4 above 7.31 in
stiffer than a dressed 2x4 above 9.14 in
stiffer than a FULL 2x4 above 11.00 in
and neighbouring panels never share a stick, so all 55 interior edges carry TWO sectors:
539 % of a stud's area, 452 % of its bending
Under 9.1 inches of trunk the wedge is the weaker member and this argument fails. The trees being cut are 12 to 15 inches, which is why it does not.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: Four ways up, one of them free
scenes.summary: The wedge is not symmetric, so which way it faces is a decision.
scenes.purpose: The wedge is not symmetric, so which way it faces is a decision.
narration: A sector has a point, two flat sawn faces and a curved bark back. Rotate it about its own long axis and you have four distinct positions in the wall.

The way to read them is to look at a pair either side of one seam. The points can face into the dome together, out at the sky together, apart into their own panels, or in toward each other across the seam.
It costs nothing to choose. Same stick, same wood, turned before it goes down.
But the choice changes how deep the section is in the direction the shell actually bends.
equations: points in, points out, points apart, points together
same wood, different depth under load

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: A panel that cannot fall through
scenes.summary: Point the wedge outward and the opening tapers.
scenes.purpose: Point the wedge outward and the opening tapers.
narration: Here is the part that made me stop thinking of these as struts and start thinking of them as a chassis. Turn every member so its pith faces out and its fat bark faces in.

The opening in the middle of each triangle is now wider at the outside than the inside, because each member gets wider as it goes inward. A panel dropped in from outside seats on that taper and is physically stopped.
It is a keystone. Which means a panel is not cladding.
It is a swappable module. You want an air conditioner: you attach one to a panel and swap the panel.
Shelving, glazing, a vent, a whole fitted appliance -- all of it becomes something you pop in and out.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: A vein through the whole shell
scenes.summary: The same rotation leaves a duct along every seam.
scenes.purpose: The same rotation leaves a duct along every seam.
narration: That rotation does something else for free. With the points facing out, the two sawn faces either side of a seam open away from each other, and they leave a continuous V running the length of every seam in the dome.
Every seam meets every other one at a vertex, so it is not a set of grooves. It is one connected network through the entire shell.
Fill it with key and it is a joint. Leave some of it and it is a duct: air moved between outside and inside, water, wire, pipe, run anywhere on the building without cutting into anything structural.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: Four rotations, four buildings
scenes.summary: Where the panel is caught, where the services run, what the saw does.
scenes.purpose: Where the panel is caught, where the services run, what the saw does.
narration: Stiffness was one axis of this choice and it is already covered. Here are the others, measured off the same cross-section.
Point out and a panel is caught from outside with the conduit in the weather. Point in and it is caught from inside with the services in the warm.

Turn it sideways and the opening goes parallel: no lip, panels held by fixings, but the sawn faces come much closer to flat, which is what sheathing wants to land on. And one of the four does something I did not expect until the solve printed it.
Turned sideways with the points facing each other across the seam, the butt cut's bevel goes to zero. The hardest cut in the build becomes a plain mitre.
equations: stiffness is one axis of the choice and it is already covered.
here is what each rotation does to the BUILDING:
S  2.05 in3   depth 4.00 in   butt bevel +22.50 deg
lip -1.53 in -- panel goes in from INSIDE and cannot fall out
seam V 22.5-27.0 deg, 3.3 in2 -> 7.1 cu ft of continuous conduit
sawn faces sit 67.5 deg off the dome surface
S  1.63 in3   depth 3.06 in   butt bevel -67.50 deg
no lip: opening is parallel-sided, panels held by fixings
seam opens to 153-157 deg: a shallow dish, not a duct
sawn faces sit 22.5 deg off the dome surface
S  2.05 in3   depth 4.00 in   butt bevel -22.50 deg
lip +1.53 in -- panel drops in from OUTSIDE and cannot fall through
seam V 63.0-67.5 deg, 7.3 in2 -> 15.6 cu ft of continuous conduit
sawn faces sit 67.5 deg off the dome surface
S  1.63 in3   depth 3.06 in   butt bevel  +0.00 deg
no lip: opening is parallel-sided, panels held by fixings
seam opens to 153-157 deg: a shallow dish, not a duct
sawn faces sit 22.5 deg off the dome surface
so: DOME-OUT catches a panel from OUTSIDE like a keystone, and puts 16 cu ft of conduit out there too
DOME-IN catches it from INSIDE and runs the services in the warm
PANEL-IN and PANEL-OUT present the flattest wood to sheathing, 22.5 deg off the surface
PANEL-OUT makes the hardest cut in the build a plain mitre, bevel 0.0 deg
Four rotations, four different buildings out of one stick: where the panel is caught, which side the services run, what sheathing lands on, and how hard the one difficult cut is.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: What the rotation is worth
scenes.summary: The same area, turned four ways, measured each time.
scenes.purpose: The same area, turned four ways, measured each time.
narration: A shell member is pushed in and out along the dome's own radius, so the stiffness that matters is measured in that direction. Turn the sector and the area does not move by a thousandth of an inch, because rotating a shape does not add wood to it.
The section modulus moves a great deal. Pointing the wedge at the centre of the dome, bark out at the weather, is the position that puts the most depth where the bending is.
It also puts the densest outer wood on the wet side and leaves both flat sawn faces where the seam key wants them.
equations: the wedge is not symmetric, so which way it faces is a decision.
turn it about its own long axis and the SHAPE stays the same
while the STIFFNESS does not, because bending in a shell is
radial: in and out along the dome's own radius.
a pair at one seam: both points inward, toward the centre of the dome
a pair at one seam: points apart, each into the middle of its own triangle
a pair at one seam: both points outward, away from the centre, at the sky
a pair at one seam: points toward each other, across the seam
area is 6.28 in2 in all four -- rotation moves no wood
but S runs 1.63 to 2.05 in3, a factor of 1.25
Pointing the wedge at the dome's centre puts 1.25 times the bending stiffness under the same wood, for free, by turning the stick before it goes down.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: A dome from whatever the woodlot gives
scenes.summary: I need a house, not a reference standard for symmetry.
scenes.purpose: I need a house, not a reference standard for symmetry.
narration: Everything so far assumed one trunk diameter. Trees do not sort themselves, and mine run ten to fifteen inches.
So solve the same dome at both ends of that range. What moves is much less than you would think, and what does move lands somewhere harmless.
Not one angle changes. The fold between panels is a property of the subdivision and has never heard of the log.

What changes is how far each member sits back from its ideal edge, and therefore how wide the key between two panels has to be -- which is the one part that was already variable. The surface ends up slightly restless where a thin member meets a fat one.
I am building somewhere to live, not something a friend can hold a straightedge against.
equations: 10-15 in logs, not one angle changes

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: What actually moves
scenes.summary: The same shell solved at both ends of the range.
scenes.purpose: The same shell solved at both ends of the range.
narration: The fold angles come out identical to six decimal places at both ends, which is the whole argument in one line: the geodesic solution does not know what a log is. The blank length barely shifts.

The offset and the key take up the rest, and the key was already absorbing the dihedral spread, so it is doing one more job it was already shaped for. And the strength question is settled by the thinnest member on the building, not the average.
At ten inches a sector still clears the crossover, so every log in the range is stiffer than the stud it replaces.
equations: the rest of this film assumes one trunk diameter. Real trees run 10 to 15 in and do not sort themselves.
solve the same dome at both ends of that range and see what moves:
fold angles: 18.029 to 22.459 deg at 10 in
fold angles: 18.029 to 22.459 deg at 15 in
IDENTICAL. not one angle in the shell depends on the log size,
because the dihedral is a property of the subdivision
member sits back from its ideal edge, further by 0.96 in on the fat logs
key base 1.95-2.33 in thin, 2.93-3.50 in fat
blank length shifts by 0.76 in across the whole range
outer surface steps by up to 2.50 in where a thin member meets a fat one
and the strength question is settled by the THINNEST member present:
= 187 % of a dressed 2x4's area and 131 % of its bending
and 10 in clears the 9.14 in crossover, so the whole range does
Mixing 10 to 15 inch logs changes no angle, moves the blank by 0.76 in, and lands the rest in the key. You get a shell with a slightly restless surface and a house that is entirely sound.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: Why there is a key in every seam
scenes.summary: Put the variation somewhere it is cheap to be wrong.
scenes.purpose: Put the variation somewhere it is cheap to be wrong.
narration: Neighbouring triangles in a geodesic shell meet at an angle, and it is not the same angle everywhere. That fold is what makes the thing a dome instead of a floor.

Because each panel carries its own member, a seam is two raw sawn faces looking at each other with a gap between them, and the gap changes seam by seam. You can close it by shaving the wood to suit each neighbour, which is a different bevel every time.
Or you can leave the structure alone and put the variation into a small tapered part that is not holding the building up.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: The angle nobody wants to cut
scenes.summary: Better in a cheap part than in every stick.
scenes.purpose: Better in a cheap part than in every stick.
narration: Here is the fold at every interior seam, and what is left over after two forty-five degree faces have folded toward each other. The spread is small in degrees and enormous in workshop terms, because it is a setup change on a saw, repeated once per seam, cut into structural members that are then not interchangeable.
Moving that variation into the key means the wood stays generic and the fussy part is small, cheap and replaceable.
equations: two panels meeting along one edge are not in the same plane.
the fold between them runs 18.03 to 22.46 deg
a spread of 4.43 deg across 55 interior seams
each panel brings its own member, so a seam has two raw sawn
faces 45 deg apart before anything folds
after folding, the gap left between them runs 22.54 to 26.97 deg
which is exactly 45 deg minus the fold
there are only two ways to close a gap that is never the same:
shave the wood to suit each seam -- a different bevel, 55 times
or leave the wood alone and fit a key that varies instead
the key's base runs 1.56 to 1.87 in
one part, cut on a taper, doing what would otherwise be a setup change per seam
The key exists so the 4.43 degrees of dihedral variation live in a small replaceable part instead of in every structural member of the building.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: One flat board, forty panels
scenes.summary: The jig is not a drawing aid. It is what makes them identical.
scenes.purpose: The jig is not a drawing aid. It is what makes them identical.
narration: The fixture is a flat board with the panel's triangle struck on it once, three rails, six little plates and some clamps. The rails set each member across the panel by its sawn point line, never by its bark, because the bark is the part of a log that is different every time.
The red and green plates do something a drawing cannot. A sector dropped in rotated ninety degrees still looks plausible; against these plates it physically will not seat.
The fixture refuses the mistake instead of relying on someone noticing it.
equations: rails on the sawn point, not the bark

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: The cut that is never measured
scenes.summary: One end arrives finished. The other arrives too long, on purpose.
scenes.purpose: One end arrives finished. The other arrives too long, on purpose.
narration: The two ends of a member are made in completely different places. The butt is cut before assembly, off the jig, to the angle its neighbour presents.
It is the same cut for every member of a family, so it batches. The head is not cut at all.

It arrives long, hangs off the board, and stays long while all three butts are pulled up tight and the pinwheel closes. Only then does a saw run flat along the fence and take the head off at the plane the neighbouring member has already established.
Nothing is measured, and every error in stock length or butt angle walks away in the offcut instead of accumulating around the triangle.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: What the fixture is enforcing
scenes.summary: Twelve steps, three constraints, and the offcut that buys accuracy.
scenes.purpose: Twelve steps, three constraints, and the offcut that buys accuracy.
narration: The fixture holds three things and nothing else: where the member sits across the panel, which way up it is turned, and the plane its head will be cut to. It is worth being precise about what the offcut buys.
Every stick has some error in it. Cut both ends to a measurement and those errors add up around the triangle until the last corner does not close.
Cut one end in place, against the neighbour, and the error has nowhere to accumulate. It leaves in the piece that falls on the floor.
equations: 40 triangles, 120 members, 120 corner joints -- all off one flat board
the fixture comes in 12 steps and holds three things:
a RAIL per member, set to the sawn point-axis, not the bark
a RED and a GREEN plate that make a wrongly-turned wedge physically refuse to seat
a FENCE at each head end, which is the plane the saw runs on
each member arrives with ONE cut already made:
the butt, cut to the angle its neighbour presents, batched
and one deliberate error: the head is left 6 in too long
three butts are pulled up, the loop closes, and only then is
each head sawn against its fence -- unmeasured, in place
the offcut is 60 ft per dome = 8.3 % of raw length
and 40 panels need only 4 physically different fixtures
Leaving 8.3 percent of the length as offcut is what buys the accuracy: error in stock length or butt angle leaves in the offcut instead of accumulating around the triangle.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: What two trees make
scenes.summary: The building at the end of all of that.
scenes.purpose: The building at the end of all of that.
narration: So this is what the arithmetic buys. Two pines off the property, converted with a chainsaw and a flat board, become a shell you can stand up in.

The floor area, the height and the member count all fall out of the longest useful piece the trees give, rather than the other way round. The building is sized by the wood, not the wood by the building.
That inversion is the part I would most like to hand to somebody else, because it is what makes the whole thing available to anyone with a saw and some trees.

scenes.title: The dome the trees size
scenes.summary: Solved backwards from the longest member the wood gives.
scenes.purpose: Solved backwards from the longest member the wood gives.
narration: Normally you pick a dome diameter and then go and find members long enough for it. This is the same solve run the other way: start from the piece the tree actually yields and ask what shell that makes.
The chord factors do not change, so the radius, the floor area and the member count all follow from one length.
equations: the tree sets the strut length, so it also sets the dome:
12 ft section, cut once = 6 ft members
the longest pinwheel member is 72.0 in
solve for the radius that makes that true:
160 - 120 = 40 left for the floor and the fit-out
timber standing in the frame = 672 ft of member
Two trees, 120 members, a 22 foot dome with 380 square feet of floor -- and 40 sticks still spare.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: The shape is doing the work
scenes.summary: None of this is a claim that split wood is better wood.
scenes.purpose: None of this is a claim that split wood is better wood.
narration: A wedge from a small tree is not a stronger stick than a stud. It is a cheaper stick, a faster stick, a stick that leaves far more of the tree standing as structure instead of as shavings, and a stick that can be made without owning a factory.
From a big enough tree it is also simply the stronger stick, and I gave you the diameter where that flips. But what makes it sufficient either way is the building.
A triangulated shell puts its members mostly in axial load, doubles every interior edge, and asks only that the ends can be made to meet. So the honest version is not that I found a better board.
It is that I picked a building that does not need one.

scenes.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scenes.title: The whole argument on one page
scenes.summary: Wood, machines, hands, rate, value, cost, strength, angle and cuts.
scenes.purpose: Wood, machines, hands, rate, value, cost, strength, angle and cuts.
narration: This is everything the film just showed, in the order it showed it, with the number attached to each line. One line still carries a condition rather than a boast: below about nine inches of trunk the single wedge is the weaker member and this stops working.
That stays on the page. Change the assumptions and the money moves.
Change the log or the dome and the geometry moves with it, because all of it is computed and none of it is typed in.
equations: WOOD     88 % of the tree kept split, 45 % sawn -- 1.95x
MACHINE  3 fewer: SAWMILL, EDGER, PLANING MILL
HANDS    15 middle men removed between tree and wall
RATE     6 wedges/hour measured, 5 used for planning
VALUE    $10.00 of wood per wedge, $45/hour net of fuel
COST     $120 to cut this dome's frame against $1476 to buy it
STICK    226 % of a dressed stud in bending at 12 in trunk; under 9.1 in it would lose
EDGE     every interior edge carries two, 539 % of a stud's section
ANGLE    4.43 deg of dihedral variation lives in the key, not the timber
CUTS     one batched butt per member, one flush cut in place, 4 fixtures for 40 panels
Not one of those lines works on a rectangular building. They work because a triangulated shell will take any stick whose ends can be made to meet, and a split log is already that stick.

scenes.title: Frequency, and where the dome gets cut
scenes.summary: Even frequencies stop at the equator. Odd ones do not.
scenes.purpose: Even frequencies stop at the equator. Odd ones do not.
narration: Raising the frequency buys a smoother shell and charges you in

hundred and fifty in six.
But there is a second effect almost nobody mentions, and the
model shows it plainly. An even frequency puts a ring of hubs
exactly on the equator, so the dome stops at half a sphere and
its height equals its radius. An odd frequency has no such
ring, so the cut lands above the equator and the building
stands taller than a hemisphere, carrying extra skin you did
not ask for.

scenes.title: A zome is not a piece of a sphere
scenes.summary: It is a shape you sweep, and that changes everything about building it.
scenes.purpose: It is a shape you sweep, and that changes everything about building it.
narration: A geodesic dome starts with a sphere and chops it into triangles. A zome
starts somewhere else entirely: you pick a handful of directions and sweep
the shape out along them, one after another. What you get is a room built
entirely from parallelograms, with a true point at the top, and it can be
framed from a single length of stick.
equations: one strut length, one point on top
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The sweep, in four steps
scenes.summary: A point becomes a stick, a stick becomes a panel, a panel becomes a room.
scenes.purpose: A point becomes a stick, a stick becomes a panel, a panel becomes a room.
narration: Take a point and drag it along the first direction: you have drawn a stick.
Drag that stick along the second direction and it sweeps out a panel. Drag
the panel along a third and you have a solid. Keep going for as many
directions as you chose, and the surface of the result is your building.
Every step of that is something you can do with your hands, and it is the
only construction rule in this lesson.
equations: sweep along g1, then g2, then g3, ...
the result is called a zonohedron
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Every panel is flat, guaranteed
scenes.summary: Two directions define a plane, so the panel they sweep cannot be warped.
scenes.purpose: Two directions define a plane, so the panel they sweep cannot be warped.
narration: This is the zome's quiet advantage over a hexagon dome. Each panel comes
from exactly two directions, and two directions define a plane, so all four
corners of that panel lie in one flat sheet. Not approximately. Exactly, and
at every size. You can cut a zome's panels from rigid sheet goods and they
will lie down without springing, complaining, or leaving a gap at one corner.
equations: planar by construction, at any size
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Make the directions equal and you get one strut
scenes.summary: A parallelogram with equal sides is a rhombus, and a rhombus needs one length.
scenes.purpose: A parallelogram with equal sides is a rhombus, and a rhombus needs one length.
narration: Nothing so far forced the directions to be the same length. If they differ,
the panels are general parallelograms and your cut list has several lines on
it. Make every direction the same length and every side of every panel is
that length, so the entire frame comes off one saw setting. This is a
decision you make once, at the very start, and it pays for itself all the
way through the build.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The star of directions
scenes.summary: Space them evenly around a cone and the whole building falls out of two numbers.
scenes.purpose: Space them evenly around a cone and the whole building falls out of two numbers.
narration: For the classic pointed zome, arrange the directions evenly around a vertical
axis, all leaning in at the same angle. That angle is the pitch, and it is
your only shape control. How many directions you use sets how many sides the
building has. Two numbers, a count and an angle, and everything else in this
lesson is derived from them.
equations: two numbers set the whole building
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Counting the parts before you buy anything
scenes.summary: Panels, struts and hubs are all simple formulas in the number of directions.
scenes.purpose: Panels, struts and hubs are all simple formulas in the number of directions.
narration: Each pair of directions makes exactly two panels, one on each side of the
building, so the panel count is n times n minus one. Each panel has four
edges and every edge is shared, so the strut count is twice that. Add the two
points and you have the hub count. Check it against Euler's formula and it
comes out to two every time, which is how you know you have not miscounted.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The top comes to a point
scenes.summary: One vertex is reached by travelling along every direction, so the roof closes there.
scenes.purpose: One vertex is reached by travelling along every direction, so the roof closes there.
narration: Walk along all of the directions in turn and you arrive at one particular
corner: the far end of the whole sweep. Only one corner can be reached that
way, so the roof closes on a single point, with one panel arriving from each
direction. Add up the panel corners that meet there and they come to less
than a full turn. That shortfall is exactly why it closes into a peak instead
of lying flat.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The hubs land on level rings
scenes.summary: Every corner at a given height is at exactly that height. No tape needed.
scenes.purpose: Every corner at a given height is at exactly that height. No tape needed.
narration: Here is the property that makes a zome pleasant to build. A corner's height
is just the number of directions you travelled to reach it, times the rise of
one direction. Every corner reached in the same number of steps is therefore
at exactly the same height, so the hubs sit on perfectly level rings, evenly
spaced. A hexagon dome has nothing like this, and it is why a zome wall meets
a floor and a lintel so easily.
equations: corner height = steps x rise per direction
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: How many panel templates
scenes.summary: Directions one apart, two apart, and so on -- and the far pairs repeat.
scenes.purpose: Directions one apart, two apart, and so on -- and the far pairs repeat.
narration: A panel's shape depends only on how far apart its two directions sit around
the star. Neighbouring directions give a long thin rhombus; opposite ones
give a fat near-square. Because a pair separated by three steps one way is
separated the other way by the same amount, the shapes pair up, and a zome
with n directions needs only about half that many templates. Cut one jig per
shape and trace the rest.
equations: separation s and n-s are the same shape
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Pitch is the free design knob
scenes.summary: Tall spire or low saucer, same struts, same count, same cut list.
scenes.purpose: Tall spire or low saucer, same struts, same count, same cut list.
narration: Lean the directions in steeply and the zome climbs into a spire. Open them
out and it settles into a wide saucer. Nothing about the strut length or the
part count changes; only the panel angles do. That means you can shape the
building to the site, the snow load, or the headroom you want without adding
a single line to the cut list. Very few structural systems give you a free
knob like this.
equations: pitch changes shape, not part count
still one strut length at every pitch
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The joints are where a zome gets particular
scenes.summary: One strut length, but several different hubs, and they are not interchangeable.
scenes.purpose: One strut length, but several different hubs, and they are not interchangeable.
narration: The saving on struts is real, but it is paid back at the joints. The corners
come in a handful of types: some take three struts, some four, and the two
points take one from every direction. Each type has its own splay angles, so
a hub that works at mid-height will not sit right near the top. Make a full
set of angle jigs before you fabricate any of them, and stamp each hub with
its type as it comes off the bench.
equations: hub types vary; strut length does not
each type has its own splay angles
stamp the type on the hub at the bench
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Meeting the floor
scenes.summary: A zonohedron has no horizontal strut, but its floor line is one repeated cut.
scenes.purpose: A zonohedron has no horizontal strut, but its floor line is one repeated cut.
narration: Not one strut in a zome runs level, so a level floor line always crosses
struts in mid span. On a polar zome that turns out not to matter: because
every hub in a ring is at the same height, the level line meets every strut
it crosses at exactly the same place along its length. One angle, one length,
repeated all the way round. Mark one, check it, then use it as the master.
equations: level line crosses every strut identically
one cut setting for the whole bottom row
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The whole cut list
scenes.summary: One stick length, a handful of panel templates, and a hub schedule.
scenes.purpose: One stick length, a handful of panel templates, and a hub schedule.
narration: This is what the shop actually receives. A single strut length, cut as many
times as there are struts in the roof, less the connector allowance you
measured on a real joint. A template for each panel shape. And a hub schedule
listing how many of each type. Everything on this list came from the two
numbers you chose in chapter five, so if you change your mind about pitch,
the list regenerates rather than needing to be re-derived.
equations: one length x every strut in the roof
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: The famous one-panel zome
scenes.summary: Thirty identical golden rhombi, and their diagonals land exactly on phi.
scenes.purpose: Thirty identical golden rhombi, and their diagonals land exactly on phi.
narration: There is one zome where every single panel is the same shape: build the star
from the six five-fold axes of an icosahedron and you get the rhombic
triacontahedron. Thirty faces, all identical, all rhombi, and the ratio of
each panel's diagonals is the golden ratio, exactly. One strut length and one
template for the entire surface. It is the most economical shell in this
whole series of lessons.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: What the golden zome charges you
scenes.summary: Its hub rings are not evenly spaced, so the floor line stops being simple.
scenes.purpose: Its hub rings are not evenly spaced, so the floor line stops being simple.
narration: The catch shows up the moment you try to stand it on something. Its rings of
hubs are not evenly spaced, so a level line through the middle of the
building meets struts at two different points along their length, and the
bottom row needs two cut settings instead of one. That is a real cost, and it
is the exact mirror image of the polar zome's trade: one pays at the panel
bench, the other at the floor.
equations: polar zome pays at the panels instead
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Raising it, tier by tier
scenes.summary: The geometry hands you the build sequence: one complete ring at a time.
scenes.purpose: The geometry hands you the build sequence: one complete ring at a time.
narration: Set out the bottom ring on a level base and bolt it down. Then add complete
tiers, never a single column of panels up one side, because a zome is a
shell and it is not stable until each ring closes. Prop the tier you are
working on until the ring above it goes in. Check the diameter of each
completed ring in three directions before starting the next, and leave the
apex panels for last.
equations: prop each tier until the ring closes
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Doors and windows
scenes.summary: Take out a whole panel and no strut needs cutting.
scenes.purpose: Take out a whole panel and no strut needs cutting.
narration: Because the frame is a net of complete rhombi, the natural opening is one
whole panel. Leave the panel out, frame the rhombus, and hang a door or a
fixed light in it: the structure is untouched. If you need something square,
build a small dormer forward out of the rhombus rather than cutting struts
out of the shell, and keep the shell's own net intact behind it.
scenes.progress_note: Editorial still default; adjust the snapshot position to reveal the intended beat.

scenes.title: Zome against geodesic dome
scenes.summary: Both close. They close for completely different reasons.
scenes.purpose: Both close. They close for completely different reasons.
narration: A geodesic dome closes because triangles hold their shape and its corners
are missing a little angle each. A zome closes because a swept solid has to
come back on itself. The dome gives you a shallower shell and famously stiff
triangulation; the zome gives you fewer strut lengths, guaranteed flat
panels, level hub rings, and vertical-ish walls that furniture can actually
stand against. Pick by what your building has to do, not by which is rounder.

scenes.title: The whole transformation
scenes.summary: A star of directions, swept out, and closed on a point.
scenes.purpose: A star of directions, swept out, and closed on a point.
narration: Pick a count and a pitch. Sweep the shape along that star of directions.
Every panel arrives flat, every strut arrives the same length, the hubs land
on level rings, and the roof closes on a single point. Cut the building off
at whichever ring gives you the room you want, and the bottom row is one
repeated cut. That is the entire method, and every number in this lesson was
recomputed from it rather than read off a table.

concepts.name: Phi places the corners, not the struts
concepts.claim: The golden ratio builds an icosahedron's twelve corners; a 2V dome's two strut lengths are not in the golden ratio.
concepts.explain: The icosahedron's corners sit on three golden rectangles, so phi really is in the shape. But a 2V dome's struts come from splitting each edge in half and pushing the midpoints out to the sphere, and that step, not phi, decides their lengths.

concepts.name: Projection makes exactly two lengths
concepts.claim: Push a split icosahedron's midpoints out to the sphere and every edge of a 2V hemisphere falls into just two lengths.
concepts.explain: Splitting each edge in half leaves the new points inside the sphere. Moving them out onto it changes the distances, and when every edge is measured they group into two classes and no more.

concepts.name: A triangle cannot change shape
concepts.claim: A triangle cannot change shape without a side changing length, so a frame of triangles holds its shape with no bracing.
concepts.explain: Four hinged sides fold into a lozenge; three cannot, because three lengths fix a triangle completely. A dome is triangles curved round in every direction, so the whole shell is braced by its own shape.
concepts.caveat: Geometry explains why the shape stands; it does not size the members. Joints and foundations still need engineering.

concepts.name: Start from the icosahedron
concepts.claim: Of the five regular solids, the icosahedron starts closest to a sphere.
concepts.explain: It has the most faces of the regular solids, so its corners are already spread most evenly over a ball, and the correction to reach a true sphere is the smallest.

concepts.name: Solve at radius one, then scale
concepts.claim: Work every length out on a sphere of radius one; one multiplication then sizes the dome to any radius.
concepts.explain: On a unit sphere every strut length is a pure factor. Multiply the factors by the real radius and the cut list appears, in any unit, for any size.

concepts.name: Only two fold angles close the dome
concepts.claim: The wedge dome's 55 seams close at only 2 fold angles.
concepts.explain: Each seam is where two panels meet at an angle. Solved seam by seam, those angles come in just two values, so two key profiles close the whole shell.
recipe: tally:{{seam.count_a}} at {{seam.fold_a_deg}} deg + {{seam.count_b}} at {{seam.fold_b_deg}} deg = {{frame.seams}} seams

concepts.name: Every hexagon cage needs twelve pentagons
concepts.claim: A sheet of hexagons stays flat forever; to close into a ball it needs exactly twelve pentagons, however many hexagons it has.
concepts.explain: Three hexagon corners use up a full circle, so the sheet cannot curve. Each pentagon leaves a gap that lifts it, and the gaps only add up to a closed ball when there are twelve.
recipe: diagram:a flat hexagon sheet curling up as pentagons replace hexagons

concepts.name: A zome's panels are flat by construction
concepts.claim: Two directions define a plane, so every panel a zome sweeps is flat, and equal directions give a single strut length.
concepts.explain: A zome is swept from a star of directions rather than cut from a sphere. Each panel is made of two of those directions, which cannot warp, and when the directions are equal the panel is a rhombus with one side length.
recipe: diagram:two direction vectors sweeping out a rhombus

concepts.name: A ring multiplies small errors
concepts.claim: Errors in a ring of struts add up as they go round; on the dome's base ring a strut error comes back amplified by the golden ratio.
concepts.explain: A ring has nowhere to put a small mistake except into the next piece, so mistakes accumulate around it. That is why a build is checked member, triangle, ring, radius and height, in that order, before the crown.
recipe: type:ERRORS ADD UP ROUND A RING

concepts.name: The shape does the work, not the stick
concepts.claim: A triangulated shell loads its members mostly in compression and tension, so it needs sticks whose ends meet, not perfect boards.
concepts.explain: A beam in a house bends under load, so it needs a strong, true section. A dome's triangles send load along their members instead, and every interior edge is doubled, so a raw wedge is enough.
concepts.caveat: From a small log a single wedge is the weaker stick in bending: -33 percent against a dressed two-by-four at 8 inches.

concepts.name: Above a certain trunk, the wedge is stiffer
concepts.claim: Stiffness grows much faster than size, so above some trunk diameter one wedge out-stiffens a dressed two-by-four.
concepts.explain: A section's resistance to bending grows with roughly the cube of its size. A small wedge loses to the board; a big one wins; the crossover diameter is where they tie.
concepts.caveat: Below the crossover the wedge is the weaker stick, and the films say so with the number on screen.

concepts.name: Forty frames, each finished on the ground
concepts.claim: Each triangle is built flat and finished before it meets its neighbours, so all the precise work happens at waist height.
concepts.explain: The frame is 40 independent panels of 3 members each. They are made one at a time on the jig, then lifted whole, rather than assembled stick by stick in the air.

concepts.name: Neighbours never share a stick
concepts.claim: Every interior edge carries two members, one from each panel, so the frame has 120 members for 65 edges.
concepts.explain: Because each panel keeps its own three members, two of them lie side by side along every shared edge, with a key between. That doubling is what lets a panel be finished on its own.
concepts.caveat: It costs more wood and more cuts than a hub dome. The trade is no hubs and no shared bevels.

concepts.name: The joint with no mitres in it
concepts.claim: In a pinwheel panel each member's end butts into the side of the next, so no end is mitred, coped or shaved to a point.
concepts.explain: The three members chase each other round the triangle the same way. The mathematical corners are reference points no stick reaches, and each end bears on a flat sawn face.
concepts.caveat: There is still one compound cut per member, the butt cut. An earlier film said there was none, and a later chapter corrects it on camera.

concepts.name: Let the key hold the angle
concepts.claim: A key in every seam takes up the angle between panels, so the variation lives in one cheap part instead of in every stick.
concepts.explain: Cutting each seam's angle into the wood would mean a different bevel on every member. A spline, hose or gasket between the panels absorbs it instead, and the wood stays raw.

concepts.name: Four ways up, four buildings
concepts.claim: A wedge is not symmetric, so the way it is turned in its panel is a design decision, and each rotation gives the frame a different feature.
concepts.explain: Point the wedges one way and the panel openings taper so a panel cannot fall through; turn them another and every seam becomes a channel for services. Same sticks, different building.

concepts.name: Short members forgive defects
concepts.claim: A defect ruins the length that has to be thrown away around it, so short members lose little to a knot or a bend.
concepts.explain: On a long board, one bad spot condemns the whole board. Bucked to 6 feet, the same spot costs one section, and even a crooked farm tree gives structure above and below its bend.

concepts.name: A split log keeps most of itself
concepts.claim: Split along its radius, a trunk keeps 87.4 percent of its wood; the only loss is the kerf.
concepts.explain: Every split follows the grain through the pith and removes only a saw's width. Of the 318 board feet in the book's trunk the cuts take 40, and the wedges keep the rest.
concepts.caveat: Recovery measures volume, not quality: a split stick keeps its knots.

concepts.name: Waste is the wrong shape, not bad wood
concepts.claim: A round log packed with rectangles loses its corners, and those corners are good wood of the wrong shape.
concepts.explain: A mill has to square a circle before it can make boards, so the slabs, edgings and shavings go. Nothing is wrong with that wood; it failed a geometry test, not a strength test.
concepts.caveat: The packing comparison is made on the films' log, which is not the book's tree; the two recoveries are different cuts of different trees.

concepts.name: One eighth of a tree, used as a stick
concepts.claim: A member is literally a sector of the trunk: pith edge in, bark face out, two flat sawn faces.
concepts.explain: Nothing about it is milled. The densest wood ends up on the weather side, the deep dimension faces the load, and its section is worth 1.23 nominal two-by-fours.

concepts.name: The tree sizes the building
concepts.claim: Buck to the longest length the trunk gives and the dome's radius, floor and height all follow: you find out the size instead of choosing it.
concepts.explain: The section length is the longest member the frame may have. Solve the dome backwards from it and the book's trees give 365 square feet under a 21.6-foot shell.

concepts.name: Or start from the dome you want
concepts.claim: Pick a floor area and the method gives the longest member, the bucking length, the sections and the trees: 300 square feet needs 2 trees.
concepts.explain: Floor area sets the radius; the radius sets the longest member; that sets the bucking length, and the sections and trunk feet follow. It is the tree-first method run the other way.
recipe: tally:{{method_a.sections}} sections of {{method_a.buck_ft}} ft = {{method_a.trunk_ft}} ft of trunk

concepts.name: The two methods are one calculation
concepts.claim: Run design-first and tree-first against each other and they close on the same dome, to within 0.0e+00 inches.
concepts.explain: One function maps a radius to a longest member and another inverts it. Feeding either method's answer into the other gets back where it started, which is the proof that neither is a rule of thumb.
recipe: diagram:two arrows between radius and longest member, closing

concepts.name: Two trees, one frame
concepts.claim: 2 trees give 128 struts for a frame that needs 120, with 8 to spare.
concepts.explain: Each tree is 8 sections of 8 struts. The spares cover the pieces a knot or a bad split spoils.

concepts.name: Fewer operations, fewer machines
concepts.claim: From standing tree to member in the frame takes 8 operations; from tree to graded board takes 14, and the board still has to be bought and cut.
concepts.explain: Every conversion step between a log and a rack is a machine, a building and somebody's wages. Splitting skips the squaring, resawing, edging, drying and planing entirely.
concepts.caveat: The two lists do not end in the same place. Counted to the same finish line the gap is wider, but the films print both lists rather than claim it.

concepts.name: The jig, not the tape measure
concepts.claim: One flat bench holds every part in the same place, so forty panels come out the same without measuring any of them.
concepts.explain: Repeatability beats accuracy when there are many of something. The jig fixes where each member sits and where each cut falls, so a mistake would have to be made the same way forty times to matter.

concepts.name: Cut it too long on purpose
concepts.claim: Leave the head end long, flush-cut it in place, and the error leaves as an offcut instead of building up round the triangle.
concepts.explain: Each member arrives 6 inches long at its head. On the jig the long end is cut off level with its neighbour, so the panel is true whatever the stick's length error was.

concepts.name: The compound cut needs two saws
concepts.claim: A hubless strut end carries two angles: the table saw rips the bevel, and a crosscut sled makes the end angle, because no mitre saw reaches it.
concepts.explain: Each machine can do only the cut the other cannot. The bevel decides how a triangle meets its neighbour; the end angle decides how a strut meets the other two in its own triangle.
recipe: diagram:the blade tilt beside the sled fence angle

concepts.name: Turn it, do not flip it
concepts.claim: The second end of a strut is not a mirror of the first: rotate the strut end for end, never face over face.
concepts.explain: Flipping it keeps the angle and puts the bevel on the wrong side, and the strut refuses to close its triangle, though it looks right on the bench.
recipe: diagram:a rotation arrow about the strut's long axis

concepts.name: The hinge steers the tree
concepts.claim: A face notch and a back cut leave a hinge of uncut wood, and the hinge, not the saw, steers the tree down.
concepts.explain: The notch opens on the side the tree should fall. The back cut frees it from the other side, and the strip between them bends instead of breaking, holding the tree to the stump as it goes over.
concepts.caveat: Felling is the most dangerous part of the whole build; the book puts its safety page before the notch.

concepts.name: Buck and split: a tree becomes struts
concepts.claim: Cut the trunk into 8 sections and split each into 8, and one tree is 64 struts.
concepts.explain: Bucking makes the lengths; three rip passes per section make the eighths. The section length is the strut length, so there is no crosscut after the split.

concepts.name: The harvest, in days
concepts.claim: The whole harvest takes 8 days of the 14-day fortnight: 2 felling, 2 bucking and 4 ripping.
concepts.explain: The day plan is a decision, but it is held to the arithmetic: the ripping block is exactly the afternoons the measured cutting rate needs, and the fortnight ends on the declared build length.

concepts.name: A few gallons of fuel, shown as a range
concepts.claim: Ripping the whole frame burns 48 tanks of fuel, between 3.6 and 4.7 US gallons.
concepts.explain: The burn rate was measured in a timed session and the hours come from the measured cutting rate. Only the saw's tank size is a guess, so the answer is a range instead of a point that pretends to know it.
concepts.caveat: Felling and bucking were never metered and are not in the figure, and the tank size still has to be read off the actual saw.
recipe: tally:{{fuel.tanks_per_hour}} tanks an hour x {{fuel.rip_hours}} hours = {{fuel.rip_tanks}} tanks

concepts.name: Raise it one complete ring at a time
concepts.claim: Never build up one side: the shell is not stable until a ring closes.
concepts.explain: Each ring braces the one below it only once it is complete. Built up one side, the frame is a leaning partial arch; built ring by ring, it is a smaller finished shell at every stage.

concepts.name: Openings come out as whole panels
concepts.claim: Doors and windows go where whole panels come out; cutting through a member means replacing a load path.
concepts.explain: Every member is part of the network that holds the shell up. Taking out a complete panel removes a triangle the rest can bridge; cutting a stick in half removes a path the load was using.

concepts.name: Close the measurement loop
concepts.claim: Check member, triangle, ring, radius and height, in that order, and fix an error before the crown.
concepts.explain: A good build is calculated, made, measured and corrected. Each check catches what the one before it would have passed on, and the last one, the height, is the dome telling you whether the sphere closed.

concepts.name: Skin it from the rim upward
concepts.claim: Lay the covering so that every lap sheds water downhill.
concepts.explain: Start at the bottom and work up, each piece lapping over the one below, like shingles on a roof. Water then runs over every joint instead of into it.
recipe: diagram:overlapping laps, water running over each joint

concepts.name: A standing frame is not a home
concepts.claim: The fortnight ends with a frame, not a shelter: skin, openings, weather and services all come after.
concepts.explain: The frame is the part the method changes. Everything that makes it a place to live is ordinary building work, and the book gives it its own part rather than pretending it is included.

concepts.name: A shelf price is mostly not the tree
concepts.claim: Stack up who takes what between a standing tree and the rack, and very little of a board's price is the wood.
concepts.explain: Logger, hauler, mill, dryer, grader, distributor, retailer: each handles the board and takes a share. The why film lists them one by one rather than quoting a round number.

concepts.name: What an hour at the log is worth
concepts.claim: Valued by the boards it replaces, an hour of cutting is worth 31.14 dollars against dressed two-by-fours.
concepts.explain: It is a substitution value, not a wage: 5.0 struts an hour, each worth the store boards of the same section and length.
concepts.caveat: Against nominal two-by-fours it is 20.43 dollars. The book prints both and says which question each answers.

concepts.name: The part nobody counts
concepts.claim: Buying lumber carries costs that never appear on the receipt: trips, culls, waiting, and boards that never make it.
concepts.explain: They feel like part of life, so nobody times them. Counted, they add real money and real hours to the store-bought side.

concepts.name: Measured and guessed, kept apart
concepts.claim: Every money figure comes after a table that says which inputs were measured and which were assumed.
concepts.explain: A number is only as good as what it rests on. Putting the measured and the guessed side by side before any money is discussed lets a viewer disagree with an assumption and still follow the arithmetic.

concepts.name: Dome labour is a flat rate
concepts.claim: Floor area grows with the radius, but the parts list does not: the same number of struts frames a small dome or a large one.
concepts.explain: The work is counted in pieces and operations, and those stay fixed as the dome grows. What changes is how long each piece is.

concepts.name: Same floor, less building
concepts.claim: A dome covers a floor with less outside surface than a box of the same floor, and the wall you never build never costs anything.
concepts.explain: A sphere encloses the most volume for its surface. Half of one, standing on a floor, needs noticeably less skin, framing and weatherproofing than a box doing the same job.

concepts.name: The brim is already a gutter
concepts.claim: An overhanging brim throws water clear of the joints and collects it at the same time.
concepts.explain: Without an overhang, rain runs down the shell into every joint at the base. With one, it drips clear, and a gutter along the brim sends it to a tank.
recipe: diagram:rain running off the brim into a tank

concepts.name: One tube, one blower
concepts.claim: A ring duct round the base and one blower move air through the whole dome, either way round.
concepts.explain: Blow in and the building breathes out through its skin; pull out and the same ring becomes a central vacuum. The flow is computed; whether the wall filters is not proven.

concepts.name: The energy claim this project will not make
concepts.claim: Less skin per floor is real, but a flat promise of lower energy bills is a claim this project refuses; its own model is shown instead.
concepts.explain: How much a dome saves depends on insulation, climate, site and systems. The presentation shows one modelled build and names the popular percentage it will not repeat.

concepts.name: The finished-home number is the honest one
concepts.claim: Stripped to a bare shell a dome is much cheaper to build; finished with the same kitchens and baths, most of that gap closes.
concepts.explain: Kitchens, bathrooms and mechanicals cost the same whatever shape the walls are. The bare-shell comparison measures the shape; the finished-home one measures the house, and it is the one to trust.
concepts.caveat: The bare-shell figure flatters the dome, and the presentations show it only beside the finished one.
recipe: type:THE SMALLER NUMBER IS THE TRUSTWORTHY ONE

concepts.name: More room for the same money
concepts.claim: The real win is volume: the same footprint and budget enclose more space inside a dome.
concepts.explain: Once the house is finished the costs are close, so the argument moves from price to what the price buys: height and air a box of the same floor does not have.

concepts.name: The curved-wall answer is a straight core
concepts.claim: Put plumbing and power in one straight column and the round walls never have to meet a pipe.
concepts.explain: The first objection to a round room is always where the plumbing goes. Concentrating every straight line in one core answers it, and leaves the curved shell to be a shell.

concepts.name: Where a dome actually wins
concepts.claim: Starter homes, backyard units, rural and off-grid sites and disaster-prone low-rise; not dense cities, and the project says so.
concepts.explain: A claim small enough to defend beats a large one nobody believes. The market-fit presentation names where the case holds and where it does not.

concepts.name: The lending door is already open
concepts.claim: Mainstream mortgage guidance already allows dome-secured loans, so financing is paperwork, not a barrier of principle.
concepts.explain: A buyer needs a lender before an argument about geometry. The financing presentation computes a real payment and points at the guidance that already covers it.

concepts.name: A home that meets you halfway
concepts.claim: One level, one ramp and one open room make a dome a natural fit for someone with limited mobility.
concepts.explain: There are no interior bearing walls to squeeze a hallway between, so the whole floor is turning space, and the rigid shell can carry a hoist or a grab bar anywhere.

concepts.name: Nothing on screen is typed in
concepts.claim: Every figure a film shows is computed by code that also proves it, and a figure that cannot be computed is declared, with its reason, on screen.
concepts.explain: A film that asserts numbers cannot be checked; one that computes them can be re-derived by anyone. The same functions feed the films, the book and the tools, so they cannot disagree.

concepts.name: Every frame is a pure function of time
concepts.claim: The same moment always draws the same picture, so a still is exact and a render is repeatable.
concepts.explain: Nothing accumulates between frames. Ask for any second of any chapter and the painter draws it from scratch, which is how a single still can be checked before a ninety-minute render.

concepts.name: From a triangle to a lit pixel
concepts.claim: A frame is a chain of small calculations: world, camera, projection, the divide, the viewport, depth and light.
concepts.explain: Each step is simple on its own, and each is computed on screen in the from-scratch film with the renderer's own settings read back out of its code.
recipe: diagram:a vertex travelling world, camera, clip, screen

concepts.name: Figures arrive with the words that say them
concepts.claim: A callout lands on the phrase that says it, and a tally builds its sum a row at a time, checked so it cannot show arithmetic that does not work out.
concepts.explain: The voice track is synthesized first and timed sentence by sentence; every figure is a token resolved from the same functions the book uses; and a column that said eight times eight is sixty-five would refuse to build.

concepts.name: Render beats, not films
concepts.claim: A film is rendered as beats, so fixing one chapter costs one short render instead of the whole film.
concepts.explain: Sections and whole films are joins of the beats, not new renders, so a corrected beat folds back in at every level in seconds.

concepts.name: Corrections belong on camera
concepts.claim: When a published film is wrong, the fix is a chapter that names the error and corrects it, not a silent re-cut.
concepts.explain: The wedge film once said the joint needed no compound cut. The why film has a chapter that says so, shows the cut, and then the number that rescues the method.
recipe: type:THE CUT I SAID DID NOT EXIST

concepts.name: Build the skeleton once, keep the bones
concepts.claim: Treat a dome as a platform you keep upgrading rather than a house you finish once.
concepts.explain: The frame lasts; the skins, services and fittings change. Swap the insulation, add the solar, reskin it for a new use, and the bones stay where they are.

concepts.name: When the material is scrap, failure is cheap
concepts.claim: Building from salvage makes experiments cheap enough to fail, which is what makes them worth running.
concepts.explain: The frankendome's brackets came out of a washing machine. A mistake in scrap costs an afternoon, not a lumber order, so the next attempt comes sooner.

concepts.name: Send it to one person
concepts.claim: One share from somebody with reach does more than a month of cutting in a field.
concepts.explain: Every film ends with the same small ask, packaged once as a segment so nobody maintains nine copies of it.
